The total electricity consumption of street lighting in a city is very high. Street lighting is often the first or second largest local government energy use (ACEEE, 2015), typically accounting for 25% to 50% of a municipal energy bill (Berg, 2012). For example, in Quezon City, Philippines, street lighting constituted 65% of the city’s electricity costs and 5% of its overall budget. In India, street lighting electricity and maintenance costs can consume 5% to 10% of municipal budgets in large cities and up to 20% in smaller cities (Li & Makumbe, 2017). Efficiency improvements to outdoor lighting offer a significant value proposition for both municipalities and electric utilities. Therefore, many countries worldwide are increasingly interested in applying new street lighting technologies for the purpose of reducing energy consumption costs without compromising the safety benefits. Many local authorities in England and Wales have reduced street lighting at night to save money and reduce carbon emissions. No empirical evidence to date has been found on whether these reductions impact public health in any way (Steinbach, 2015). The effects of four street lighting adaptation strategies were quantified on casualties and crime in England and Wales. These included switching lights off permanently (“switch off”), reducing the number of hours that lamps are switched on at night (“part-night” lighting), reducing the output of lamps at night (“dimming”), and replacing traditional sodium lamps with more energy efficient lamps or LEDs (“white light”). Specifically, 859,935 collisions in the 62 local authorities during 2000–2013 were included in the analysis. As shown in Figure 4, there was no evidence from any of the regional models, or the overall estimates, for an association between any street lighting adaptation strategy and a change in collisions at night (Figure 4).
